builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted model uses more compute or memory than your workload can justify.
builder_plan.change: Check for a usable pruned checkpoint and runtime support before attempting model surgery.
builder_plan.baseline: The original unpruned model at the same precision, context, and load.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task quality, actual GPU memory, serving throughput, and preparation cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
summary: The paper proposes an evaluation framework that measures information preservation as similarity preservation for binary sparse codes, intended to replace ad-hoc or absent quantitative comparisons of sparse coding methods; it does not introduce a new production inference method to replace an existing component in an LLM stack. Applying the framework costs implementation and benchmarking effort across multiple coding models, and adopting binary sparse representations can impose additional encoding/decoding complexity and potential accuracy loss relative to dense representations. The reported trade-off can fail to yield a practical benefit in deployment if the achievable sparsity does not translate into end-to-end latency or energy gains on the available 24 GB GPU or API-based pipeline.
rationale: The contribution is primarily an evaluation framework plus comparative findings for sparse coding methods, with no demonstrated production-ready improvement that the reader can deploy under constrained infrastructure.
technique: Binary sparse codes with similarity-preservation metrics

claims.statement: The paper proposes an evaluation framework that measures information preservation as similarity preservation for binary sparse codes, intended to replace ad-hoc or absent quantitative comparisons of sparse coding methods; it does not introduce a new production inference method to replace an existing component in an LLM stack. Applying the framework costs implementation and benchmarking effort across multiple coding models, and adopting binary sparse representations can impose additional encoding/decoding complexity and potential accuracy loss relative to dense representations. The reported trade-off can fail to yield a practical benefit in deployment if the achievable sparsity does not translate into end-to-end latency or energy gains on the available 24 GB GPU or API-based pipeline.

The paper reports a trade-off in which models with high information preservation sacrifice sparsity; Competitive Sparse Codes is identified as the only architecture occupying a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. No multiplicative improvement factor over a production baseline is stated.
